title: India's GST collections just posted their fastest growth of the fiscal year. November 5, 2026.
excerpt: From a decisive 1817 battle near Pune, to an Apple executive born in Moradabad now running its global supply chain, to GST collections growing faster than any month this fiscal year, to a dairy farmer who turned 3 cows into a Rs 14 lakh income - November 5's four stories are about momentum building in quiet, unglamorous ways.
bodyHtml:
Every story today is about something building momentum away from the spotlight - a battle that reshaped a map two centuries ago, a supply chain running behind every iPhone, a tax number tracking real economic activity, and a herd of cattle that grew one cow at a time.

A battle near Pune decided the fate of an empire that had ruled for over a century

The Battle of Khadki was fought November 5, 1817, near Pune. East India Company forces defeated the army of Peshwa Baji Rao II in a decisive early battle of the Third Anglo-Maratha War, leading directly to the fall of the Peshwa and British annexation of Pune.

He was born in Moradabad. Now he runs Apple's entire global operation

Sabih Khan became Apple's Chief Operating Officer, succeeding longtime COO Jeff Williams. Born in 1966 in Moradabad, Uttar Pradesh, he joined Apple in 1995 and now oversees its worldwide operations, supply chain, and AppleCare - called by Tim Cook 'a brilliant strategist.'

India's GST collections just posted their fastest growth of the fiscal year

India's net GST collections rose 25.6% year-on-year to Rs 2.03 lakh crore in October 2026 - the fastest net growth of FY27 so far, driven largely by import-linked GST up 42.2%, with domestic GST growing a steadier 15.8%.

She started with 3 cows and limited market access. A year later, she'd earned Rs 11.5 lakh

Kaushalya Devi, from Barhi village in Gorakhpur district, joined a women-led dairy cooperative under the National Rural Livelihood Mission. She now owns 14 cattle, supplies 70 litres of milk daily, and was personally acknowledged by PM Modi as a 'Lakhpati Didi.'

Four stories, one pattern: an empire that fell two centuries ago, a supply chain quietly running the world's most valuable company, a tax number tracking an economy's real pulse, and a herd that grew from three cows into a six-figure income.
